19366:
Theodore Beza (1519–1605). Profession: lawyer, poet, then theologian, professor and Calvin's successor as leader of Geneva's pastors. Born at Vézelay in Burgundy, he studied law and wrote fashionable Latin poetry in Paris before a serious illness and conversion led him to Geneva in 1548. He taught Greek in Lausanne, became first rector of the Geneva Academy in 1559, defended the French Protestants at the Colloquy of Poissy (1561), published editions of the Greek New Testament, and led Geneva's church for four decades after 1564. Beza set out predestination in a more logical, system-like way (his 1555 chart of predestination is famous) and leaned toward 'supralapsarianism', the view that in God's plan the decree to elect comes logically before the decree to permit the fall. Historians debate whether this was a departure from Calvin or a natural development.

In the Netherlands, followers of the Leiden professor Jacobus Arminius issued the 'Remonstrance' of 1610: five articles teaching election based on foreseen faith, an atonement intended for all, the need for grace, grace that can be resisted, and uncertainty about whether true believers can fall away. The Dutch Reformed Church called an international synod at Dordrecht (Dort), November 1618 to May 1619, with delegates from Britain, the German territories and Switzerland. Its *Canons of Dort* answered the Remonstrants point by point under five 'heads of doctrine': unconditional election, an atonement effective for the elect, human corruption, effectual grace, and perseverance.

The synod's aftermath was harsh: some two hundred Remonstrant ministers were deposed, many exiled, and in a related political struggle the statesman Johan van Oldenbarnevelt was executed (May 1619) and Hugo Grotius imprisoned. The Remonstrants were tolerated again from the 1630s.

The word TULIP came much later. No sixteenth- or seventeenth-century writer used it, and its order does not even follow Dort's. The earliest known uses date from the early twentieth century in American Presbyterian circles; historian Kenneth Stewart traces it to around 1905–1913.
19367: Myth: 'Calvin invented the five points of TULIP.' Calvin died in 1564; the five points come from the Synod of Dort's reply to the Remonstrants in 1619, and the TULIP acronym is an early-twentieth-century teaching device. Calvin's own views on the extent of the atonement are still debated by historians.
19369:
The Puritans were English (and later New English) Protestants who wanted the Church of England more fully reformed. Their theology was mostly Reformed, and they wrote some of its most searching pastoral literature. William Perkins (1558–1602), a Cambridge preacher and theologian, became the most-read English theologian of his generation and wrote at length on how a person can know they are elect. John Owen (1616–1683), Oxford vice-chancellor, chaplain to Oliver Cromwell and later a nonconformist pastor, wrote *The Death of Death in the Death of Christ* (1647), the classic defence of definite (limited) atonement, and still-loved works on sin and communion with God. The Westminster Assembly's Confession of Faith (1646–47) became the standard for Presbyterians worldwide. Not every Puritan was a strict Calvinist; Richard Baxter (1615–1691) held a moderate, more universal view of the atonement.

Jonathan Edwards (1703–1758). Profession: pastor, revival preacher, philosopher-theologian, missionary and briefly college president. Born in East Windsor, Connecticut, educated at Yale, he succeeded his grandfather Solomon Stoddard as pastor in Northampton, Massachusetts. Revivals broke out there in 1734–35 and again in the Great Awakening of 1740–42, when he worked alongside the English evangelist George Whitefield; his sermon 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' (1741) is famous, though most of his preaching dwelt on God's beauty. His *Religious Affections* (1746) tried to tell true conversion from emotional excess. Dismissed by his church in 1750 after a dispute over who could take communion, he became missionary pastor to Mohican and Mohawk people at Stockbridge, where he wrote *Freedom of the Will* (1754), arguing that people always choose according to their strongest desire, so they are free and responsible even though their choices are certain. He became president of the College of New Jersey (Princeton) in 1758 and died weeks later after a smallpox inoculation. He also owned enslaved people, which recent historians and admirers alike treat as a serious moral failure.
19371:
Charles Hodge (1797–1878). Profession: seminary professor and theologian. Born in Philadelphia, he taught at Princeton Theological Seminary for more than fifty years, training thousands of Presbyterian ministers. His three-volume *Systematic Theology* (1871–73) set out a confident, carefully argued Calvinism for the American church, and he edited the influential *Princeton Review*.

B. B. Warfield (1851–1921). Profession: seminary professor, theologian and New Testament scholar. Born near Lexington, Kentucky, he taught at Princeton from 1887 until his death. He is best known for defending the inspiration and inerrancy of Scripture and for *Counterfeit Miracles* (1918), the classic statement of cessationism, and he wrote widely on Calvin and Augustine. He spent much of his married life caring for his invalid wife, Annie, and was more open to some form of evolutionary biology than many later conservatives assume.

Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834–1892). Profession: Baptist preacher, pastor, author and founder of institutions. Born in Kelvedon, Essex, he was converted at sixteen in a small Methodist chapel in a snowstorm, became pastor of New Park Street Chapel in London at nineteen and drew such crowds that the Metropolitan Tabernacle was built (1861). He never attended university, founded a Pastors' College and the Stockwell orphanage, and his sermons sold in their millions. Spurgeon was a convinced Calvinist who fought 'hyper-Calvinism' and pleaded with every hearer to come to Christ. He left the Baptist Union during the 'Downgrade Controversy' (1887–88) over what he saw as drift from biblical truth, and he lost American sales for preaching against slavery.

D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones (1899–1981). Profession: physician, then preacher and pastor. Born in Cardiff and raised in Wales, he trained at St Bartholomew's Hospital in London and became assistant to the royal physician Sir Thomas Horder before leaving medicine in 1927 to pastor a mission church in Aberavon, South Wales. From 1939 to 1968 he preached at Westminster Chapel in London, where his long expository series on Romans and Ephesians became classics. He helped revive interest in the Puritans (with the Banner of Truth publishing house), urged evangelicals in 1966 to leave doctrinally mixed denominations (a public disagreement with John Stott), and, unusually for a Calvinist, taught that a distinct baptism with the Spirit was available to believers.
19372: Myth: 'Calvinists don't evangelise.' Hyper-Calvinists such as some eighteenth-century English Baptists did hold that preachers should not urge the unconverted to believe. Mainstream Calvinists, from Whitefield and Spurgeon to Lloyd-Jones, rejected hyper-Calvinism and preached for conversions.
19374:
In the early 2000s a wave of younger American evangelicals, many of them Baptists or non-denominational, embraced Reformed theology. Journalist Collin Hansen called them 'Young, Restless, Reformed' in a 2006 *Christianity Today* article and 2008 book, and *Time* magazine listed 'the New Calvinism' among ideas changing the world in 2009. Networks such as The Gospel Coalition (founded 2005), Together for the Gospel and Desiring God gave it shape. It mixed Puritan-style doctrine with modern worship music, church planting and online teaching.

John Piper (born 1946). Profession: pastor, author and former biblical studies professor. Raised in South Carolina, he studied at Wheaton and Fuller and earned a doctorate in Munich, taught at Bethel College, then pastored Bethlehem Baptist Church in Minneapolis from 1980 to 2013. *Desiring God* (1986) taught 'Christian hedonism': God is most glorified in us when we are most satisfied in him. His ministry Desiring God is among the movement's most influential.

Timothy Keller (1950–2023). Profession: Presbyterian (PCA) pastor, church planter and apologist. From Allentown, Pennsylvania, he pastored in Virginia and taught at Westminster Theological Seminary before founding Redeemer Presbyterian Church in Manhattan in 1989, which grew among young urban professionals. *The Reason for God* (2008) became a bestseller; he co-founded The Gospel Coalition and helped plant hundreds of churches. He died of pancreatic cancer in May 2023.

R. C. Sproul (1939–2017). Profession: theologian, teacher, author and pastor. From Pittsburgh, he founded Ligonier Ministries in 1971, wrote *The Holiness of God* (1985) and *Chosen by God* (1986), and taught millions through radio and video. John MacArthur (1939–2025). Profession: pastor, Bible teacher and seminary president. Pastor of Grace Community Church in Sun Valley, California, from 1969, he founded The Master's Seminary and produced the *MacArthur Study Bible*. He combined Calvinist salvation teaching with dispensational views of prophecy and strong cessationism (*Strange Fire*, 2013), so he is better described as an elder ally of the movement than a 'New Calvinist' himself.

The movement has also faced criticism, including from inside: high-profile leadership failures (for example the collapse of Seattle's Mars Hill Church in 2014), disputes over complementarianism, and charges of tribalism. Supporters point to renewed seriousness about doctrine, preaching and church planting.
19376:
T, Total depravity. Not 'everyone is as bad as possible', but 'sin has touched every part of us', mind, desires and will, so that left to ourselves we do not truly want God (Rom 3:10-12; Eph 2:1-3). People still do kind and admirable things; they simply cannot make themselves love God. Other traditions often agree with this point but add that God's grace already reaches out to everyone to free the will enough to respond.

U, Unconditional election. Before creation God chose particular people to save, not because he foresaw their faith or goodness, but out of his free mercy (Eph 1:4-5; Rom 9:11-16). Faith is the result of election, not its cause. The alternative ('conditional election') says God chose those he foreknew would believe (Rom 8:29; 1 Pet 1:1-2).

L, Limited atonement, which most Calvinists prefer to call 'definite' or 'particular redemption'. Christ's death was sufficient for all but intended to secure the salvation of the elect; he laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:11; Eph 5:25). Many Calvinists, the 'four-pointers' or 'Amyraldians', reject this point. Non-Calvinists hold Christ died for everyone (1 John 2:2).

I, Irresistible grace, better called 'effectual calling'. When God sets out to bring someone to new life, his Spirit does not fail; he changes the heart so that the person comes willingly (John 6:37; John 6:44). It does not mean people are dragged in against their will, nor that no one ever resists the Spirit for a time. The alternative says grace enables but can finally be refused (Acts 7:51).

P, Perseverance of the saints. Those God truly saves he keeps, and they will continue in faith to the end, not because they are strong but because he holds them (John 10:27-29; Phil 1:6). It is not 'once saved, always saved no matter how you live': Calvinists say real faith shows itself in a changed life. Arminians and Wesleyans hold that a true believer can fall away (Heb 6:4-6).
19377: Myth: 'Total depravity means people are incapable of any good.' Calvinist confessions affirm that unbelievers do many good things through God's common grace; the claim is that no part of human nature is untouched by sin and that no one, unaided, turns to God in faith.
19378: Positive impacts, as adherents and many historians argue
19379:
Assurance and comfort. Calvin treated election as good news for anxious believers: if salvation rests on God's choice and not on our performance, it cannot be lost by our weakness (Rom 8:31-39). Many Calvinists testify that this gave them peace in suffering and persecution, from French Huguenots to modern believers.

God-centred worship and seriousness. Reformed churches stressed preaching through whole books of the Bible, psalm-singing, and a vision of all life lived 'to the glory of God' (1 Cor 10:31). Calvinism has produced a large literature of hymns, devotional writing and theology.

Education. Calvin's Geneva Academy (1559), the Scottish parish-school ideal, Dutch universities and early American colleges such as Harvard, Yale and Princeton drew on the Reformed conviction that every believer should read Scripture and that all knowledge belongs to God.

Missions. The modern Protestant mission movement owes much to Calvinists. William Carey (1761–1834), a Particular (Calvinistic) Baptist shoemaker-turned-pastor, wrote his *Enquiry* in 1792 and sailed for India the next year; his friend Andrew Fuller had argued that the gospel should be offered to all. David Brainerd, Henry Martyn and many Presbyterian and Dutch Reformed missionaries followed. Calvinists argue that confidence God has his people 'in every nation' fuels mission rather than killing it (Acts 18:9-10; Rev 7:9).

Political theory and work. Because Calvinists believed every ruler is under God and no human is sinless, many argued for limits on power: Beza's *Right of Magistrates* (1574), Samuel Rutherford's *Lex, Rex* (1644) and later Abraham Kuyper's idea of 'sphere sovereignty' (that family, church, state and school each have their own God-given authority). Some historians link these ideas to constitutional government and resistance to tyranny. The sociologist Max Weber famously proposed in 1904–05 that a Puritan 'work ethic', partly driven by the search for signs of election, helped give rise to modern capitalism; that thesis remains contested and many economic historians reject it in its strong form.
19380: Often-told story: when young William Carey proposed foreign mission at a ministers' meeting, an older minister told him to sit down because God would convert the heathen without his help. The story comes from later family recollections and its wording is uncertain; even if it happened, Carey's own Calvinist circle went on to found the Baptist Missionary Society.
19382:
Fatalism. Critics say that if God has settled everything, prayer, evangelism and moral effort lose their point. Calvinists answer that God ordains means as well as ends, so prayer and preaching are the very ways his plan comes about (Westminster Confession 3.1 and 5.2), and that fatalism is a misunderstanding; the hyper-Calvinist minority who stopped inviting sinners proves the danger is real, though.

Assurance anxiety. Ironically, a doctrine meant to comfort could also torment. Later Puritan writers taught believers to examine their lives for evidence of election, and some fell into deep doubt about whether they were among the chosen. Historian R. T. Kendall argued (1979) that this came from a shift between Calvin and later Calvinists; others, such as Paul Helm, dispute that reading. Ex-Calvinists today often report similar fears.

Harshness and the Servetus legacy. Critics point to Servetus, to strict church discipline in Geneva and Scotland, and to a reputation for severity and joylessness. Defenders reply that other confessions were no gentler and that Reformed piety has also produced deep warmth and joy.

Apartheid theology, debated. In South Africa, leaders of the Dutch Reformed Church (NGK) gave theological backing to racial separation, drawing on ideas of distinct peoples and spheres associated with neo-Calvinism. Historians debate how far this was Calvinism and how far nationalism using Christian language. It was also Reformed Christians who led the opposition: Beyers Naudé, Allan Boesak and others; the World Alliance of Reformed Churches declared apartheid a heresy in 1982, and the Belhar Confession (1982, adopted 1986) rejected it on Reformed grounds.

Church splits and tribalism. The Synod of Dort ended with Remonstrant pastors deposed; George Whitefield and John Wesley split over predestination in the 1740s; many Presbyterian and Baptist bodies divided over these questions; and recent Southern Baptist life has seen bitter disputes. Critics say Calvinism breeds argument and pride in doctrinal precision; Calvinists reply that clarity about the gospel is worth contending for, while admitting that some adherents have been needlessly combative.
19383: Whether these harms flow from Calvinist doctrine itself or from human sin that would have found other excuses is exactly what the two sides dispute. Fair readers will notice that many of the strongest critics of each abuse were themselves Calvinists.
19384: The verses Calvinists rely on: Romans 9
19385:
Romans 9 is the chapter both sides know best. Paul is grieving that most of Israel has not believed in Jesus and asks whether God's word has failed (Rom 9:1-6). He answers that not all descended from Israel are 'Israel': God chose Isaac, not Ishmael, and Jacob, not Esau, before the twins were born or had done good or bad, so that God's purpose in election might stand, not because of works but because of him who calls (Rom 9:6-13). God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills (Rom 9:18). When someone objects, 'then why does he still blame us?', Paul answers with the image of a potter who has the right to make vessels for honour and for dishonour (Rom 9:19-23).

The Calvinist reading: Paul is explaining why some individuals believe and others do not, and his answer is God's free choice. The objections Paul anticipates ('is God unjust?' 9:14; 'who can resist his will?' 9:19) only arise if he is teaching unconditional election; if election were based on foreseen faith, the obvious answer would be 'no, God chose those who would believe', which Paul never gives. Corporate groups are made of individuals. Key defenders: Augustine, Calvin, John Piper (*The Justification of God*, 1983), Thomas Schreiner.

The non-Calvinist readings: (1) Corporate and historical: Jacob and Esau stand for nations (Gen 25:23; Mal 1:2-3), and Paul is explaining God's freedom to choose which people carry his purposes in history, now including Gentiles, not who goes to heaven. (2) The point of the chapter is that God can define his people by faith rather than ancestry, which is exactly where Paul ends (Rom 9:30-32; Rom 10:9-13). (3) The potter image comes from Jeremiah 18:1-10, where the potter reshapes a nation according to how it responds. (4) Paul says God 'prepared beforehand' the vessels of mercy, but the vessels of wrath are described with a verb many read as 'fitted' or 'ready' for destruction, perhaps by their own doing (Rom 9:22-23). (5) Romans 9 must be read with Romans 11, where hardened Israelites can be grafted back in if they do not continue in unbelief (Rom 11:23) and God has consigned all to disobedience in order to have mercy on all (Rom 11:32).
19386: Ephesians 1, John 6, Acts 13:48 and other Calvinist texts
19387:
Ephesians 1:4-11. God 'chose us in him before the foundation of the world' and 'predestined us for adoption', according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will. Calvinist reading: particular people were chosen before time, by God's will alone, and the purpose is unshakeable (Eph 1:11). Non-Calvinist reading: the key phrase is 'in him'. God chose Christ, and chose a people in Christ, the way Israel was chosen in Jacob; individuals come to share that election when they are joined to Christ by faith (Eph 1:13 'when you believed'). What is predestined is the goal (adoption, holiness), not who believes. Some Arminians instead tie election to foreknowledge (Rom 8:29; 1 Pet 1:2).

John 6:37-44 and 6:65. All the Father gives Jesus will come to him; no one can come unless the Father draws him, 'and I will raise him up on the last day'. Calvinist reading: those drawn are the same ones raised, so drawing does not fail; it is effectual and given to the elect only. Non-Calvinist readings: verse 45 explains the drawing as hearing and learning from the Father, i.e. through his teaching, which can be resisted; John 12:32 says Jesus will draw 'all people', so drawing is necessary but not by itself decisive (Wesley's 'prevenient grace'); some read 'those the Father gives' as faithful Israelites who already trusted the Father and were handed to Jesus.

Acts 13:48. When Gentiles in Pisidian Antioch heard the gospel, 'as many as were appointed to eternal life believed'. Calvinist reading: the appointment came first; faith followed. Non-Calvinist reading: the Greek participle could be read as middle voice, 'as many as were disposed (or lined up) for eternal life', contrasting with the Jewish listeners who 'judged themselves unworthy' (Acts 13:46). Most translations keep 'appointed' or 'ordained'.

Other texts Calvinists cite: John 10:26 ('you do not believe because you are not my sheep', not the other way round); Rom 8:29-30 (the 'golden chain' in which all the foreknown are glorified); Eph 2:1-9 (dead people cannot raise themselves; salvation is God's gift; both sides agree the 'gift' in 2:8 refers to the whole package of salvation by grace through faith); Phil 1:29 (it has been granted to you to believe); John 1:12-13 (born not of human will but of God). Non-Calvinists reply that 'foreknew' in Rom 8:29 implies God knew something about them, that John 10:26 describes settled unbelievers rather than the never-elect, and that 'dead' in Eph 2 is a picture of separation, not total inability.
19388: Straw men on both sides, corrected
19389:
About Calvinists. 'They believe God creates people just to damn them.' Mainstream Calvinists say every person who is lost is lost for their own sin, and God takes no pleasure in it (Ezek 33:11); they treat reprobation (God passing over some) as a mystery they speak of reluctantly. 'They think we are robots.' Calvinists hold that people choose freely in the sense that they do what they most want; they deny only that the fallen will can, unaided, want God. 'They don't care about evangelism.' See Whitefield, Carey, Spurgeon and the modern church-planting networks. 'Calvinists think they are better than others.' The doctrine teaches that the elect were chosen despite having nothing better about them (Deut 7:7-8; 1 Cor 1:26-29), though individual pride is a real risk they themselves warn against.

About non-Calvinists. 'They think people save themselves.' Arminians and others teach that no one can believe without prior grace and that faith earns nothing. 'They deny God's sovereignty or foreknowledge.' Classical Arminians, Molinists and others affirm God's complete foreknowledge and sovereign rule; only the small 'open theism' movement denies exhaustive foreknowledge, and most Arminians reject it. 'They make God the servant of human choices.' Their claim is that God sovereignly chose to create free creatures and to save those who trust him; that, they argue, is itself a sovereign decision. 'They believe you can lose your salvation every time you sin.' Wesleyans and Arminians who hold that believers can fall away usually mean deliberate, persistent rejection of Christ, not ordinary failures.

On both sides, the most respected writers agree that the other side are brothers and sisters in Christ. Wesley and Whitefield disagreed sharply but Wesley preached at Whitefield's funeral; Spurgeon called Wesley a saint while disputing his theology.
19390: Scripture by scripture: verses often raised against Calvinism, the Calvinist reply, and the non-Calvinist counter-reply
